name: Latency
summary: End-to-end freshness — the time between an event occurring and a result being available to query — where lower is better and batch cadence is the enemy.
description: Latency is how stale the data is when someone reads it, and how fast a single query returns. It is driven down by streaming and CDC that process events as they arrive, incremental computation, materialized views, in-memory serving, and pre-aggregation. Batch architectures deliberately accept high latency in exchange for simplicity and throughput, while real-time designs invest heavily to reach sub-second freshness. Latency frequently trades against throughput and cost.

mechanisms.name: Streaming and change data capture
mechanisms.note: Processing events the moment they arrive, instead of on a batch schedule, collapses freshness delay to seconds or less.

mechanisms.name: Incremental processing
mechanisms.note: Recomputing only changed rows rather than full rebuilds shortens each cycle and keeps outputs continuously current.

mechanisms.name: Materialized views
mechanisms.note: Maintaining query results incrementally as data changes serves fresh answers without recomputing on read.

mechanisms.name: In-memory low-latency serving
mechanisms.note: Keeping hot data resident in memory-optimized stores answers point lookups and dashboards in single-digit milliseconds.

mechanisms.name: Pre-aggregation and rollups
mechanisms.note: Precomputing rollups turns expensive scans into fast reads, cutting query latency at the cost of extra write work.

manifestations.statement: Fresh events stream into a memory-optimized OLAP engine with pre-aggregation, delivering sub-second dashboards and APIs on near-live data.
Every record is processed as it flows through the log, so derived views stay seconds-fresh with no batch cadence in the path.
Capturing commit-log changes as they happen gives the analytics mirror low-latency freshness far ahead of nightly extracts.
Contract-first events propagate the instant they are published, so downstream services react with minimal end-to-end delay.
Continuous small commits keep open tables minutes-fresh, giving lakehouse economics with far lower latency than batch loads.
Pre-aggregated tenant models answer in-product queries fast, but data freshness still depends on the upstream load cadence.
The speed layer serves fresh approximate results with low latency while the batch layer trails behind, so freshness is mixed by design.
An online store serves features at low latency for inference, while the offline path remains batch and lags for training data.
Telemetry streams in with low ingest latency, but end-to-end freshness depends on whether analytics reads the stream or a batched store.
Data is only as fresh as the last scheduled run, so nightly or hourly batches deliberately accept high latency for simplicity and throughput.
Dimensional loads run on batch windows, so reports reflect the previous load and cannot serve truly live data without added streaming.
The normalized enterprise core is built by periodic integration loads, prioritizing consistency over freshness and yielding high latency.
Batch bronze-to-gold promotion favors throughput and cost, so gold tables lag by the batch interval unless a streaming path is added.
Activation runs on sync schedules after warehouse loads complete, so insights reach SaaS tools well after the underlying events occurred.
Avoiding copies means each query pays cross-source network and pushdown cost at read time, trading freshness convenience for higher per-query latency.
Retrieval is fast, but LLM generation dominates end-to-end response time, so answer latency is bounded by the model rather than the data path.
Audit-oriented batch loads and the many-join read path make both freshness and query response slow without downstream marts.
Governed, policy-enforced access through a sharing gateway adds authorization and query-mediation overhead, so collaborative queries are slower than reading a local private copy.
Dynamic masking, tokenization lookups, and row-level security filters are evaluated per query, adding a governance tax that lengthens response times on sensitive data.
Definitions compile down to warehouse SQL so latency largely tracks the engine, though the abstraction can emit heavier joins than hand-tuned queries.
Pre-aggregation and tenant-scoped serving keep customer-facing dashboards fast, but strict isolation and per-tenant filtering add predicate overhead versus a single pooled query.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: Serving the freshest data means processing each event individually rather than in large batches, which lowers bulk efficiency and the total volume the system can push through.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Low latency needs always-on streaming pipelines and in-memory serving layers running 24/7, so you pay for standing capacity even during quiet periods.

tradeoffs.title: Consistency
tradeoffs.note: Racing to serve the newest data forces reads before all replicas or aggregations settle, so ultra-low latency often means accepting eventual or partial reads.

tradeoffs.title: Operational complexity
tradeoffs.note: Streaming and CDC stacks with stateful operators, watermarks, and exactly-once tuning are operationally complex to build, monitor, and recover compared with periodic batch jobs.
